clue.text: Detective — one who makes mischief

parts.note: BUSY is old British slang for a police detective
a body is a person, anyone at all

explanation.surface: A police detective turns out to be the troublemaker.
explanation.walkthrough: BUSY is a dated British slang word for a police detective; 'Detective' looks like the definition but is only the first piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A meddler who pokes into others' affairs stirs up trouble, the classic mischief-maker.

clue.text: Favourite son's predicament in African country

indicators.note: in means the predicament sits inside the country

parts.note: Benin is a country in West Africa
a jam is a tight spot or predicament

explanation.surface: A beloved son gets into trouble in Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: In Genesis Jacob's youngest son was his favourite after Joseph.
explanation.definitionFit: The youngest son of Jacob, doted upon, gives the name for a favoured youngest child.

clue.text: Consequence of firewood, surplus?

parts.note: a spill is a thin strip of wood used for lighting fires
anything over is left over, extra

explanation.surface: Asking whether excess firewood has some result.
explanation.definitionFit: An effect that spreads from one area to another is an unintended result.

clue.text: Gently sprinkle monk with water at initiation

parts.note: the Venerable Bede was an English monk and historian

indicators.note: at initiation means at the beginning, so take only the first letter of water

explanation.surface: Christening a monk with a gentle sprinkle of water.
explanation.definitionFit: To moisten with drops like dew is a light wetting.

clue.text: The German spirit, not quite in disorder

parts.note: der is a German word for the

indicators.note: not quite means the word is cut short by its final letter

parts.note: an angel is a heavenly spirit

explanation.surface: A German ghost is somewhat confused.
explanation.definitionFit: To throw something into confusion is to upset it.

clue.text: A piece, perhaps, of mental torture

indicators.note: to torture something is to twist it, so the letters of mental are twisted into a new order

explanation.surface: A small item that causes mental anguish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A piece, perhaps' is cryptic: add PIECE to the answer and you get a shelf above a fireplace.
explanation.definitionFit: Joined with the word piece it names the fireplace shelf, so it is a cryptic hint by completion.

clue.text: Fear arrest

explanation.surface: Dread of being taken in.
explanation.definitionFit: To anticipate with dread is one sense; to seize a suspect is the other.

clue.text: Follows stories when read aloud

indicators.note: when read aloud signals that only the spoken sound counts

parts.note: tales are stories

explanation.surface: Someone pursues stories by reading them out.
explanation.definitionFit: To shadow someone covertly is to track them.

clue.text: Notebook about church journal

indicators.note: about means the first piece goes round the second

parts.note: LA is a musical note and NT the New Testament, a book of the Bible
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A notebook containing details of a church magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: Split 'Notebook' into note (LA) and book (NT); they go about CE.
explanation.definitionFit: A leading British medical periodical carries this name.

clue.text: Agree to take office

explanation.surface: Consenting to assume a post.
explanation.definitionFit: To assent is one sense; to come to a throne or position is the other.

clue.text: Aquatic plant bill introduced by Bevan in speech

indicators.note: introduced by means the bill comes after, led in by the other piece
in speech means the name is spoken, so only its sound counts and the spelling changes

parts.note: Aneurin 'Nye' Bevan, the Labour politician who founded Britain's NHS
AD is short for advertisement, a bill or poster

explanation.surface: A piece of legislation about a water plant brought in by Bevan in a speech.
explanation.walkthrough: Aneurin 'Nye' Bevan was the Welsh Labour minister who founded the NHS; 'in speech' sounds his name, and 'introduced by' sets the bill after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Naias is a genus of submerged water weeds, commonly called water nymphs.

clue.text: Where guests are welcomed, at home?

explanation.surface: Asking where visitors are greeted when one is at home.
explanation.definitionFit: A hotel's front desk greets arrivals; an 'at home' is an old-fashioned party where hosts receive visitors.

clue.text: Grant a discount

explanation.surface: An instruction to give a price reduction.
explanation.definitionFit: A grant of money paid regularly is one sense; a deduction from a price for trade-ins is the other.

clue.text: Follow directions to go round university

indicators.note: to go round means these compass letters surround the other piece

parts.note: E, N, S and E are compass points, directions on a map

explanation.surface: Instructions to follow a set of directions around a campus.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that comes after as a result is said to result from it, coming next in sequence.

clue.text: How Keats wrote? Quite the opposite

explanation.surface: Asking about the Romantic poet's style, then answering with a contradiction.
explanation.walkthrough: Split it as IN VERSE: Keats was a poet, so he wrote in poetry.
explanation.definitionFit: Keats composed poetry, written in lines; and an opposite or reverse is the other sense.

clue.text: A reasoned exposition in Latin, or a translation into English

indicators.note: into English means E goes on at the end
a translation turns the words into a new form, so their letters are reworked

explanation.surface: A careful argument written in Latin, or rendered into English.
explanation.definitionFit: A logical basis set out for a course of action is its justification.

clue.text: For example, soldiers in retreat come out of hiding

indicators.note: in retreat means going backwards, so the letters of both pieces read from the end

parts.note: EG is short for exempli gratia, for example
REME is the Royal Electrical and Mechanical Engineers, a British Army corps

explanation.surface: Soldiers who were retreating come out of hiding, for instance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in retreat' turns the whole run EGREME round.
explanation.definitionFit: To appear from concealment is to surface or become visible.

clue.text: Irritate but manage to communicate

explanation.surface: Annoying someone while still making a point.
explanation.definitionFit: To annoy someone is one sense; to make yourself understood is the other.

clue.text: Blank cheque has familiar writing

parts.note: free can mean overfamiliar, taking liberties
a hand is a style of handwriting

explanation.surface: An unsigned cheque bears handwriting you recognise.
explanation.definitionFit: Unlimited licence to act as you wish, carte blanche, is the idiom.

clue.text: Scratches from honours course, say

indicators.note: say signals that the word is to be heard, not read

parts.note: Greats is the Oxford honours degree in classics

explanation.surface: Marks earned from a university honours course.
explanation.walkthrough: Greats is the informal name of the Oxford classics degree, Literae Humaniores.
explanation.definitionFit: To rasp or scrape harshly against a surface is a synonym.

clue.text: Still getting interference?

explanation.surface: Asking whether radio noise persists.
explanation.definitionFit: Motionless is one sense; crackle on a radio or television is the other.

clue.text: Accountant takes a bizarre tour round central Sardinia

indicators.note: round means the scrambled letters go around the next piece
bizarre means strange or odd, so a tour is rearranged oddly
central picks the middle letters of the word Sardinia

explanation.surface: A bookkeeper goes on an odd trip around the middle of Sardinia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'central' takes the middle pair of Sardinia, which 'round' puts inside the anagram of 'a tour' made by 'bizarre'.
explanation.definitionFit: One who examines financial accounts officially is a checker of the books.

clue.text: These days a chap can't in the end display an inflexible attitude

parts.note: AD, anno domini, marks the present era
a man is a chap

indicators.note: in the end picks the final letter of the word can't

explanation.surface: Modern men can't help being stubborn.
explanation.definitionFit: Unyielding, refusing to be persuaded.

clue.text: Contracted out

explanation.surface: Work handed to an outside firm.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a batsman caught is out.
explanation.definitionFit: Picked up an illness is one sense; dismissed in cricket by a fielder's catch is the other.

clue.text: In the morning, I leave to see a foreign friend

parts.note: AM is ante meridiem, before noon
to go is to depart or leave

explanation.surface: A traveller sets off early to visit a pal abroad.
explanation.definitionFit: Spanish for friend, a pal from abroad.

clue.text: Furious tempo after introduction to Intermezzo

indicators.note: after puts the tempo behind the opening letter
introduction to takes the opening letter of Intermezzo

parts.note: rate is speed or tempo

explanation.surface: A musical tempo marking after an opening piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Very angry, enraged.

clue.text: "Beware the awful ——" (Longfellow)

parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation from the poem Excelsior, where an old man warns the youth of a snowslide

explanation.surface: A line of verse quoted from Longfellow with its last word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: In Longfellow's Excelsior the old man warns of the mountain's dangers: beware the pine tree's withered branch, beware the awful snow-slide.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word in the quoted line is a mass of snow sliding down a mountain.

clue.text: Joint stock bank, legally incorporated

indicators.note: incorporated means contained in, so the run sits within these words

explanation.surface: A joint-stock bank registered as a legal company.
explanation.definitionFit: The joint between foot and leg.

clue.text: A state arming in turmoil about grievances

indicators.note: in turmoil means thrown into disorder, so these letters are reshuffled

parts.note: VA is the abbreviation for Virginia, a US state

explanation.surface: A country arming itself in chaos because of complaints.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' is a link: the anagram is of A, VA and ARMING.
explanation.definitionFit: A legal term (Latin plural) for the chief points of complaint in a case.

clue.text: Licence in Koran to make money

indicators.note: poetic licence allows liberties, so taking licence with the word Koran rearranges it

explanation.surface: Permission granted in a holy book to earn cash.
explanation.definitionFit: The currency of Sweden and Iceland, so a unit of money.

clue.text: Subject West End to force of law

parts.note: a theme is the subject of a talk or work

indicators.note: End picks the final letter of the word West

explanation.surface: Putting London's theatre district under police control.
explanation.walkthrough: London's Metropolitan Police are 'the Met', a police force.
explanation.definitionFit: The Metropolitan Police is London's police service, a body enforcing the law.

clue.text: Fools, possibly, withdrawing under pressure

indicators.note: withdrawing means drawing back, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: fools are fruit-and-cream puddings, so they are an example of sweets

explanation.surface: Idiots, perhaps, backing away under strain.
explanation.walkthrough: A fool is a British pudding of fruit folded into cream.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeling strain or anxiety is being tense and overworked.
